findings.title: run_brain_2.sh joins the writers' batch files with plain `cat`. This file path was never used in development, and a file without a final newline silently loses questions
findings.evidence: In development the writers returned their questions through a schema-checked structured output (the workflow script /root/.claude/projects/-home-user-integratedai-cie/275b943f-.../workflows/scripts/brain-writers-train-dev-wf_847b22c7-f99.js) and the orchestrator wrote dev5k_*.outputs.jsonl. For the test, docs/benchmarks/brain/writers_test.js has each writer use the Write tool to write its own JSONL file, and run_brain_2.sh line 20 runs `cat $O/test5k_${K}_b*.jsonl`. I took the development outputs, split them into the run_brain_1 batch names (test5k_descriptive_811_b00..b03, test5k_prose_812_b00..b05) and removed only the final newline from each file. `cat` then puts the last line of one batch and the first line of the next on one line. read_rows keeps that line as text, and _parse fails on the two objects, so both questions are rejected as 'not a JSON object'. collect kept 30 descriptive (instead of 36) and 42 free-text (instead of 52) questions, so the mix gets 42 free-text questions where the document says 50. Nothing fails: the script just prints 'kept 42 rejected 13'. Two other formats a writer might produce: a JSON array as the first batch file crashes collect with `JSONDecodeError: Extra data`, and set -e stops the run after the questions are sealed; a pretty-printed array in a later file loses the whole batch (27 kept, 42 junk rejections). Nothing checks that every batch file exists or that its line count matches the count the writer returned. With the files exactly as development wrote them, collect's output was byte-identical to the development questions files (36/4 and 52/8).
findings.fix: Replace the `cat` with `awk 1 $O/test5k_${K}_b*.jsonl > $O/test5k_${K}.outputs.jsonl` (this adds any missing final newline). Before collect, check that there are 4 and 6 batch files and that each one's line count equals the `written` count the workflow returned, and stop if not. Better still, have writers_test.js return the outputs through a schema as in development and write the file from the workflow result, so the test uses the same path as development. Say in the document what happens if a writer fails.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute how the code fails. I could only make the trigger look less likely, so I would rate this medium rather than high.

Confirmed by reading the code and re-running it:
- Development got the writers' questions back through a schema-checked structured output (outputs[] in brain-writers-train-dev-wf_847b22c7-f99.js). The test is different: writers_test.js has each writer write test_out/<batch>.jsonl with the Write tool, and run_brain_2.sh line 20 joins those files with a plain `cat`. That way of reading the questions was never used in development.
- `read_rows` in brain_writers.py tries json.loads on each line and keeps a line that fails as plain text. `_parse` then takes the text from the first "{" to the last "}". On a line where two objects were joined, that fails, so `collect` rejects both questions as "not a JSON object".
- I split dev5k's outputs into the run_brain_1 batch names (4 descriptive files, 6 free-text files) and ran collect on dev5k's packets and keys. With final newlines, the output was byte-identical to dev5k_*.questions.jsonl (36/4 and 52/8). With the final newline removed from each file, it gave 30 kept / 7 rejected and 42 kept / 13 rejected. The extra rejections are all "not a JSON object", and nothing fails.
- Downstream, `draw_questions` ("A kind with too few questions gives what it has") and `quotas` fill only what is available. So the mix silently gets 42 free-text questions where the document commits to 50. The collect report, with the rejection reasons, is sent to /dev/null, so the operator sees only the kept and rejected counts.
- `cat` over the glob also skips a batch file that does not exist. That happens if one writer agent fails, which the workflow reports as written: null. Nothing in run_brain_2.sh compares file counts or line counts with the `written` counts. Losing one 10-packet free-text batch would leave about 43 free-text questions. The document does not say what to do if a writer fails.

Evidence that the newline trigger is unlikely:
- I checked every Write call recorded in this project's transcripts: 236 of 236 ended with a newline. That includes 9 JSON files written by blind writer agents in workflows set up the same way (plan9/blind3, ord/blind5, tick/blind4/writer*.json). The files on disk end in a newline too.
- The prompt says "one JSON object per line", which makes the JSON-array and pretty-printed cases unlikely as well.

Why it should still be fixed before the freeze: the test runs only once, the loss is silent, and fixing it after the questions are sealed and scored would be a departure from the plan. The fix is cheap:
- replace the `cat` with `awk 1` (or a Python join);
- before collect, check that there are 4 and 6 batch files and that each file's line count equals the workflow's `written` count, and stop if not;
- say in the document what happens if a writer fails or if fewer than 50 free-text questions pass the checks.

Development kept 52 of 60, so a normal keep rate already leaves little room above 50.

findings.title: Rule 6 (size): the small control scores not-found questions lower because of the small bank's vocabulary, not its size, so the rule's tolerance on the other families roughly doubles
findings.evidence: Dry run (prefreeze/run/dry, report.md): v15 not_found is 1.000 at 5,000 documents and 0.800 on the 266-document small set. Four nf_person questions ('List every GitHub pull request authored by Erin Kapur...', 'Which Jira tickets are assigned to Aria Díaz?...') got route 'plan' and a made-up answer on the small set. Brain.people_asked only flags a name whose first word is a first name and whose last word is a last name of someone in the bank, and the small bank lacks those people. v15's big-minus-small for the mean over families was +0.046, and not_found alone gave +0.050 of it (single -0.006, multi 0.000, prose -0.010). So rule 6, big ≥ small − 0.05, would still be met with a real drop of almost 0.10 on the other three families. v1 shows the same effect in reverse on nf_pr (+0.15). The small-set check reported not_reproduced = {} because it checks only that the invented name is still absent, not that the brain can still detect it.
findings.fix: Compute rule 6 over single, multi and prose only, or leave not_found out of the big-minus-small difference (against_small), and say so in the rule. Or keep the rule as written and add a note that the small set's not-found score depends on which names and key prefixes the bank holds.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. The finding is confirmed in the code, in the dry run and in the development data.

What I checked:
- **Cause.** In cie/src/cie/factbank/brain.py, people_asked flags a name only when its first word is in the bank's set of first names and its last word is in its set of last names. These sets come from person_names, which reads the bank's own people.
- **How the questions are made.** missing_people in brain_questions.py builds each invented name from first and last names found across the whole 5,000-document set. The small control holds only about 260 gold documents, so one half of the name is often missing from it.
- **Dry run.** In prefreeze/run/dry, four of the five nf_person questions got route 'plan' and a made-up answer on the small set and 'not_found' on the big one: Erin Kapur, Aria Díaz, Ronan Menon and Santiago Kapoor. The report's numbers match the finding: v15 single -0.006, multi 0.000, prose -0.010, not_found +0.200, mean +0.046. So not_found alone adds +0.050.
- **Not a one-off.** I loaded a copy of the dev5ksmall v2 bank with the frozen lessons and router. Frozen v15 caught 16 of 20 not-found questions (0.80). The same four of five nf_person names slip through, each missing its first or last name from the small bank: Simran Delgado, Rae Ruiz, Tomás Marino, Kiro Murphy. The development report already shows it for v15base: single -0.042 hidden under not_found +0.200, mean +0.039.
- **The rule's code.** Rule 6 in preregistered() reads the four-family big_minus_small mean from against_small. The small-set check (not_reproduced) only confirms that the invented name is still written nowhere in the set. It does not check that the brain can still spot it, which is why it reported {}.

What it means:
- With not_found at +0.20, rule 6 is met whenever single + multi + prose together are at least -0.40, an average drop of about 0.13 per family. Without this effect the limit is -0.20, or about 0.067 per family. The tolerance roughly doubles.
- The effect always favours v15, the method under test.
- One small error in the finding: it says v1's +0.15 on not_found is "in reverse", but it is in the same direction (big higher than small). This changes nothing.

What argues against it:
- Rule 6 is only reported. It does not decide the claim, which rests on rules 1 to 4.
- The report prints the differences family by family, so a careful reader can see the effect.

Why it should still be fixed before the freeze:
- The bias is systematic, it favours the tested method, and it was already visible in development data.
- A rule cannot be changed after the freeze without it counting as a deviation.
- The fix is one line. Either compute rule 6 over single, multi and prose only, or report it both ways and add a note that the small set's not-found score depends on which names the bank holds.

I deleted the scratch copy of the bank afterwards and did not modify any repository files.

findings.title: writers_test.js says to pass 'the batch names step 1 printed', but run_brain_1.sh prints no batch names
findings.evidence: I ran run_brain_1.sh's batch step on the development packets and on a fresh dev-zone draw. It prints 'test5k_descriptive_811 40 packets', 'test5k_prose_812 60 packets' and '10'. The batch names the workflow needs as args (test5k_descriptive_811_b00..b03, test5k_prose_812_b00..b05) appear only as file names in test_batches. Passing the printed names would start 2 writers on files that do not exist (test5k_descriptive_811.json).
findings.fix: Have run_brain_1.sh print the batch names as a JSON list (for example `ls $S/brain/writers/test_batches | sed 's/.json$//' | python -c 'import sys,json;print(json.dumps(sys.stdin.read().split()))'`), and refer to that line in writers_test.js.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute it and could not. In run_brain_1.sh, the batch heredoc prints `name, len(ps), "packets"`, where name is the kind-level stem ("test5k_descriptive_811", "test5k_prose_812"). Then `ls ... | wc -l` prints only a count (10). The real batch names (`{name}_b{i//10:02d}`, so ..._811_b00..b03 and ..._812_b00..b05) are never printed. They exist only as file names in writers/test_batches.

writers_test.js line 6 says "Run as a Workflow with args = the batch names step 1 printed (files in DIR)". Each writer is told to Read `${DIR}/${b}.json`. Passing the printed stems would point two writers at files that do not exist (test5k_descriptive_811.json).

I reproduced this in scratch by running the identical heredoc on the dev packets (dev5k_descriptive_711, dev5k_prose_712). It printed "dev5k_descriptive_711 40 packets", "dev5k_prose_712 60 packets" and "10", and the batch names appeared only as the 10 files. The scratch folder is deleted.

The pre-registration doc (lines 117-118 and 130-131) gives no batch names either. So the comment is factually wrong.

Not required before the freeze, but worth the one-line fix:
- **It fails loudly.** With the wrong args, no `test5k_*_b*.jsonl` outputs are written. run_brain_2.sh's `cat $O/test5k_${K}_b*.jsonl` then fails under `set -e` before anything is scored.
- **Nothing in the test zone is exposed or biased.** Writers that hit a missing file see nothing. Re-running with the correct names is a fresh, sealed run.
- **The right args are easy to recover.** They are deterministic, and the comment's own "(files in DIR)" points at them.

Because the run scripts are listed as frozen artifacts (pre-registration line 267), a later edit would need a deviation note. Fixing it now is the cleaner option: make run_brain_1.sh print the batch names as a JSON list, or reword the writers_test.js comment to "the batch file names in DIR without .json".

findings.title: run_brain_1.sh throws away the packet reports that development kept
findings.evidence: run_brain_1.sh lines 19-22 send the packets command's report to /dev/null: packets by source and field, answer lines dropped, how many texts still give the answer, candidates. For training and development these reports were kept (docs/benchmarks/brain/development/packets_*.report.json). The draw report is kept as $T/draw_report.json, and the collect reasons survive in *.questions.rejected.jsonl, so only the packet reports are lost.
findings.fix: Redirect each packets command to $P/test5k_<kind>_<seed>.report.json instead of /dev/null. It holds counts only.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. The packets report only ever goes to stdout. In cie/src/cie/eval/brain_writers.py, packets() builds the report (by_source, by_field, candidates, left_out, avoided, used_by_questions, answer_lines_dropped, answer_in_text, text_chars) and returns it. main() writes only the packets file and the keys file, then print(json.dumps(rep)). No report file is written. cie/docs/benchmarks/brain/run_brain_1.sh lines 19-22 send both packets commands to /dev/null. The other reports do survive, as the finding says. brain_draw.draw writes out/draw_report.json (brain_draw.py:270), brain_test questions writes questions_report.json (brain_test.py:346), and the collect step's rejection reasons are kept in *.questions.rejected.jsonl. Development kept all four packets reports in docs/benchmarks/brain/development/packets_*.report.json, so the test run would be missing something development has.

What would be lost is only part of it. by_source, by_field and text_chars can be rebuilt from the saved keys and packets files. answer_in_text can too, because it is _gives_value(packet text, key expected, key type). candidates, left_out and answer_lines_dropped need the test documents again. Re-running the packets command is deterministic, but only in a folder without questions.jsonl, because once run_brain_2 writes it, used_documents() changes which packets spread() picks. So rebuilding them afterwards means reading the test documents again.

No rule, score or decision uses these counts. The pre-registration's "Also reported" list does not promise packet reports; it promises the questions set aside and the writers' rejected questions with reasons, and both are kept. So this is a real but low-severity gap in reporting, and the test is valid without the fix. Making it before the freeze is still worthwhile because it is a safe two-line change: send each packets command to $P/test5k_<kind>_<seed>.report.json. The report holds counts and paths only, and that folder already holds the keys. Changing the script after the freeze would have to be logged as a deviation.

findings.title: run_brain_2.sh takes about 66 minutes, and the CPUs are checked for idleness only once, before the arms
findings.evidence: Measured times on the dry run: collect ×2 about 1 s; questions (seed 810, with the small set) 211 s; banks 27 s (5,000 documents) plus 5 s (small); small set, all arms 354 s (quotes 4, v1 20, v2 59, v13 146, v15 125); 5,000 documents: quotes 14 s, v1 178 s, v2 386 s, v13 940 s, v15 921 s, v15 under hash seed 1 918 s; score 4 s. idle() runs once, before the arms. A job that starts later inflates the 'time per question' the document reports (v15 median 4.6 s here, which matches '3–5 seconds'). Separately, line 79 refuses a folder that already has questions.jsonl, so if any later step fails the rest has to be restarted by hand.
findings.fix: Call idle before each 5,000-document v13/v15 ask, or record /proc/loadavg in each ask. In the document, say how long the run takes and how to resume after a failed step (the commands after the questions step can be rerun one by one).

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute it and couldn't. The facts hold, apart from one wrong line number, but the issue only affects running the test and the document, not whether the test is valid.

What I confirmed:
(1) The run takes about 66 minutes. The dry-run logs in scratchpad/prefreeze/run (stage1-5.log and the arms.json files in dry/test5k and dry/test5ksmall) give these times. 5,000 documents: quotes 13.8 s, v1 178 s, v2 386 s, v13 940 s, v15 921 s, v15 under hash seed 1 917 s. Small set: 3.8 + 20.1 + 58.8 + 145.7 + 124.9 s. Add the questions step (about 211 s), the banks (about 32 s) and the score (about 4 s) and the total is about 3,960 s. FACTBANK_BRAIN_PREREGISTRATION.md never gives the total time. It only says "about 3–5 seconds per question" under Known limits, and the dry run's report.md gives a v15 median of 4,578 ms.
(2) idle() is called only once, at run_brain_2.sh line 36, after the banks and before all eleven asks (about 60 minutes of work). Even that one check doesn't guarantee anything: after 40 tries the loop falls through with status 0 and the script carries on, and it accepts load 1.x on 4 CPUs.
(3) The refusal is real, but it is at run_brain_2.sh line 17, not line 79: `test ! -e $T/questions.jsonl || exit 1`. brain_test.questions itself does not refuse. With `set -e`, a failure in a later step stops the script, and running it again is refused, so the remaining commands have to be run by hand.

Why it doesn't need fixing before the freeze:
- Time per question appears only under "Also reported" and in Known limits. None of rules 1–7 uses it.
- Answers do not depend on timing. brain.py, engine.py, plans.py, factbank_multi.py and factbank_test.py only measure time with perf_counter for the ms field. None of them has a timeout or time budget that could change an answer when the machine is busy. The hash-seed-1 check also gave identical scores in the dry run.
- Resuming works today. ask() can be run again under the same name: the registry check allows the same arm, and the label clash check skips the same name. The later commands can also be rerun one by one, or the whole run redone from a fresh folder, because the questions come from fixed seed 810.

Suggested fixes, nice to have only: record /proc/loadavg with each ask or call idle before the 5,000-document v13 and v15 asks, and add the total time (about 66 minutes) and resume instructions to the document.

findings.title: Dry run of run_brain_2.sh on development data: every step ran and all seven rules were met

Then run_brain_2.sh, changed only in the T/TS/P/O paths, ran stage by stage. No step failed. Questions: 212 (single 106, multi 36, not_found 20, prose 50, descriptive 36), small set 266 documents, not_reproduced {}. Answer files carried the labels the rules read: v1, v2, v13, v15, quotes and v15_seed1 (rule 5 leaves out v15_seed1). Mean over families: quotes 0.214, v1 0.303 (single 0.758), v2 0.237, v13 0.293 (multi 0.917), v15 0.861 (single 0.765, multi 1.000, prose 0.680, not_found 1.000, false not found 0.000, route accuracy 0.995). findings.title: Rule 3 (free text, v15 >= quotes - 0.05) sits inside sampling noise: chance can make it pass or fail
findings.evidence: I scored the saved dev5k answers (quotes.jsonl, v15b.jsonl) with brain_test.score_rows (plain_answer included). On free text v15 got 0.663 and quotes 0.654, but the two disagree on 15 of 52 questions (v15 better on 7, worse on 8). The paired per-question difference has SD 0.395, so its SE at the test's 50 questions is about 0.056, which is larger than the 0.05 margin. I resampled the dev differences at n=50 (4,000 draws, script in scratchpad/prefreeze/measure/noise.py). As observed (+0.01), the rule fails 12.9% of the time. If the true difference is 0, it fails about 17.5% of the time. If v15 is truly 0.05 worse, it still passes about half the time. The document's 'How to read differences' only describes granularity ('one question moves it by up to 0.02'). It never says the rule's margin is about one standard error.
findings.fix: Say in the document that rule 3 is decided within about one SE. Pre-register a paired bootstrap interval of v15 - quotes on the free-text family (memory_test.paired_ci already exists) and report it next to the verdict. Or, before freezing, state the rule as a lower interval bound (for example, the 95% lower bound of v15 - quotes >= -0.10) instead of a point margin.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. The numbers reproduce exactly. I ran brain_test.score_rows on scratchpad/brain/dev5k myself (with plain_answer, no stale arms). Free text has 52 questions: v15b scores 0.6635 and quotes 0.6538. They disagree on 15 questions, v15 better on 7 and worse on 8. The paired difference has mean +0.010 and SD 0.395, so its SE is 0.056 at n=50 and 0.055 at n=52. memory_test.paired_ci on the dev pairs gives (-0.096, +0.119).

My own resample of the dev differences (20,000 draws at n=50, a different seed from the reviewer's) agrees with theirs:
- at the observed difference, rule 3 fails 12.7% of the time;
- if the true difference is 0, it fails 17.5%;
- if the true difference is -0.05, it fails 48.9%, so it passes about half the time;
- if the true difference is -0.10, it still passes 19%.

The disagreements run both ways. They come from which retrieval happens to catch the right passage, not from anything systematic. So the dev SD is a fair guess for the test's 50 new writer questions.

The other rules for comparison, same method:
- Rule 1 (single, about 105 questions): SE 0.011 against a 0.03 margin, about 2.7 SE. It fails 0% at the observed difference and 0.2% at a true difference of 0.
- Rule 2 (multi): SE 0.039, but on dev v15 is never worse than v13 (CI 0.0 to 0.139), so it is not exposed the same way.

That leaves rule 3 as the one decisive rule that sits inside about one SE. The headline claim ('rules 1 to 4 all met') therefore has roughly a 13-17% chance of failing by chance alone, even if v15 matches plain search on free text.

Partial mitigations, which do not refute it:
- Known limits says 'the families are small, so one or two questions decide a close rule'.
- 'How to read differences' gives granularity only ('one question moves it by up to 0.02').
- The earlier FACTBANK preregistrations also used point margins without intervals.

None of these states sampling error. And 'What decides' reads any unmet decisive rule as 'v15 does not yet answer that kind as well', which overstates a rule-3 failure. MEMORY_TEST_PREREGISTRATION already has a house precedent for paired bootstrap intervals with a 'not clearly' label. brain_test.score computes no interval.

Must fix before freeze: yes, in the minimal form. This changes how the result is analysed and read, and adding it after the scores are seen would look post hoc. The fix is cheap:
- one sentence in 'How to read differences' saying rule 3's margin is about one SE;
- pre-register a paired bootstrap interval of v15 minus quotes on the prose family (memory_test.paired_ci), reported next to the verdict, with a 'not clearly' reading when it spans the margin.

Changing rule 3 itself to an interval bound is optional. Only scratch scripts were written, in scratchpad/prefreeze/measure_refute/ (check.py, r12.py). No repository files or test-zone data were touched.

findings.title: Rule 2 (multi) comes down to two questions; rule 1 (single) almost only checks that v15 reproduces v1
findings.evidence: Multi: about 36 questions, and one question is worth 0.028. So one net loss against v13 passes (-0.028 >= -0.03) and two net losses fail (-0.056). On dev5k v15b and v13 differ on only 2 of 36 multi questions (v15 won both). Resampling the dev differences centred on 0 fails rule 2 in about 13% of draws. The document itself names a known loss pattern: 'the other ticket linked to ENG-…', lost once on each of two earlier sets. The link group gets about 3-4 ticket_link questions (dev: 3), so two such questions in the test would fail the claim. Single: v15b and v1 differ on only 2 of 106 dev single questions (0.804 vs 0.800; one win, one loss on meeting_attendees-079). Resampled, rule 1 fails less than 1% of the time by chance. Rule 1 is robust, but mostly because v15's single answers are v1's answers. Rule 4: the not-found score needs 16 of 20. Dev gave 20/20 and 0 false not-found out of 194, and P(fail) is 0.04 at a detection rate of 0.9.
findings.fix: In 'How to read differences', state the concrete exposure: rule 2 fails on two net multi losses, about a 1-in-8 chance even at equal skill on dev's disagreement rate. Pre-register that a rule-2 failure caused by ticket_link questions is diagnosed as the known pattern. Report paired intervals for rules 1 and 2 as well.

verdict.reason:
The finding's arithmetic is correct, but the problem it claims either is already disclosed or rests on assumptions that don't hold.

Checked on dev5k by rescoring factbank.jsonl, factbank_v13.jsonl and v15b.jsonl with brain_questions.score:
- Multi has 36 questions. v15b and v13 differ on only 2 of them (parent_issue-001 and -004), and v15 won both.
- Single has 106 questions. They differ on 2: v15 loses meeting_attendees-079 and wins pr_repo-005 (0.804 vs 0.800).
- One loss in 36 passes rule 2 (-0.028) and two fail it.
- The ~13% sign-flip figure and P(fail rule 4) of about 0.043 at p=0.9 also check out.

Why this does not make a defect that must be fixed:

(1) The exposure is already in the draft. "How to read differences" says rule 2's margin "allows about one" question, and Known limits says "one or two questions decide a close rule". The fix would add a probability to a limit that is already stated.

(2) The 13% figure assumes equal skill and borrows dev's disagreement rate. On dev, both disagreements were v13 errors on parent_issue, a kind where v15 has a structural advantage. I reran the frozen lessons on the 12 earlier multi sets (guard_md.py). There, v15 and v13 differ on about 9 of about 600 questions: about 5 wins and 4 losses. At that rate, rule 2 fails about 2% of the time even at equal skill, and the expected parent_issue cushion lowers that further.

(3) The ticket_link threat does not apply to this test. run_brain_2.sh passes no --multi-wordings, so brain_questions.generate calls factbank_multi.questions with held_out=True. findings.title: Value checks accept a value anywhere in a 1,000-character answer: counts and common words score by accident
findings.evidence: brain_questions.score sends multi values to own_score, then direct, then memory_test.check, which matches (?<!\w)value(?!\w) anywhere in the line. Field kinds use value_hit and descriptive questions use direct, with the same 'anywhere' rule. Dates need an exact set of dates, and names and keys use F1, so long answers are penalised on those kinds but not on value kinds. Dev cases: quotes scored 1.0 on person_count-053 (expected '2') from '(2-3 slides)' in a non-gold document (gold not cited), and 1.0 on desc-711-027 ('procurement') without citing the gold document. v1 and v2 multi hits are the common status 'In Progress' (pr_issue-status-104/073). In dev v15b sent none (v15base sent 6 single questions to prose).
findings.fix: Note it in Known limits. Optionally, for value kinds, score a long answer (for example more than 200 characters, or any prose-route answer) by whether the value appears in the cited gold document's quote. At least report per arm how many value hits come from answers over 200 characters (score_rows already records chars).

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. The mechanism and the dev examples check out, but the effect cannot make v15 pass a decisive rule falsely.

How the scorer works (cie/src/cie/eval/brain_questions.py):
- `score` sends field value kinds and descriptive questions to `value_hit`, and multi value kinds through `own_score`, then `direct`, then `memory_test.check`.
- Both search for the value between word boundaries anywhere in `final_answer("Answer: " + answer)`.
- The quotes arm's answers are one line of about 1,000 characters, so the whole quote is searched.
- Dates must match exactly (`dates_in(line) == {date}`), keys use F1, and names use `name_f1`. So the asymmetry is real.
- `plain_answer` strips citation markers, and `summarise` reports `answer_chars`. Its docstring even says "a long answer can hold a short expected value by chance". So the harness half-acknowledges the issue, but Known limits in the preregistration covers chance matches only for free-text facts.

What the dev data shows (my script over `score_rows` in dev5k; the questions scored by value):
- **quotes:** 11 value hits (9 single, 2 multi), all from answers over 1,000 characters. person_count-053 (expected '2') is credited from '(2-3 slides)' in a non-gold document. desc-711-027 ('procurement') is credited from 'Procurement sign-off' in Vanguard Helix Analytics, not the gold Sterling Loop Solutions. Others are legitimate, such as hubspot_close-089 and desc-711-024 quoting the gold field.
- **dev5ksmall:** the same pattern, with 11 quotes hits from long answers.
- **v1, v2, v13, v15base, v15a and v15b:** no value hit from an answer over 200 characters. Every v15b and v1 hit is an answer of 1 to 28 characters that equals the value exactly.
- **Routing:** v15b sent no single or multi question to prose. v15base sent 6, which all scored 0.
- **v1/v2 multi hits:** pr_issue-status-104 and -073 are short "In Progress" answers. That is a common value matching by chance, which any exact-match scorer allows, not the long-answer problem.

What it does to the rules:
- **Rule 3:** prose is scored by `fact_share`, not by values, so the rule is unaffected.
- **Rule 5:** extra credit for quotes only raises the bar v15 must clear, so it cannot cause a false pass. Removing all 11 quotes hits would lower quotes' mean over families from 0.204 to about 0.17, against v15b's 0.867 and a required margin of 0.20.
- **Rule 1:** the effect could favour v15 only if its router sent value questions to prose. In dev it sent none, and the expected gain is well under one question at the 0.03 tolerance.

So the finding is real but low, and it does not need fixing before the freeze. It is worth a line in Known limits ("value kinds match the value anywhere in the answer line; quotes' long answers can score a value by chance"). Optionally, the report could count per arm the value hits from answers over 200 characters. The script I used for that count is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/prefreeze/measure/valhits.py.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute all four parts against the code and the development data, and all four hold. None of them changes a rule or an outcome. They are errors in the text that is about to be frozen.

(1) The doc says 'document fields: 31 kinds' (line 84). Counting brain_questions.CATALOGUE by (family, group) gives 27 kinds in ('single', 'fields'), and len(FIELDS) is 27. The mix's 'document fields' line draws from that group. The descriptive writers ask 28 (brain_writers._ASKED is FIELDS plus linear due_date). No grouping I tried gives 31.

(2) The doc says 'The rule router sent 7 free-text questions to a fact route' (line 205). The routes for prose-family questions in dev5k are:
- v15base.jsonl: fact 7, plan 1, prose 44
- v15a_rule.jsonl: fact 7, plan 1, prose 44
brain_test.route_class counts any route other than 'not_found' or 'prose' as 'fact', so 'plan' is a fact route under rule 7. The existing report.md agrees: right route 0.846 = 44/52. The same paragraph uses 'a fact route' to include plan when it says the trained router sends every single- and multi-document question to a fact route (v15a: single fact 50, plan 56; multi plan 36). So the count should be 8.

(3) I rescored every arm per question with B.score on plain_answer (scratchpad/prefreeze/measure/below.py). Against quotes, v1 and v13, the frozen v15b is below the best arm on exactly 12 questions, which matches the doc's 12 and its breakdown. Adding v2, which rule 5 counts as an 'other arm', gives 17. v2 alone beats v15b on five more:
- desc-711-016, desc-711-020, desc-711-029, desc-711-035 (v2 1.0, v15b 0.0)
- linear_due_window-007 (v2 1.0, v15b 0.667)
v2 also ties quotes on meeting_date-054. So '12 of 214 ... the best other arm' quietly leaves out v2.

(4) The doc says free text is scored by whether facts appear 'word for word' (line 240). The scorer is brain_questions.fact_share, which calls evidence_audit.present: every number in the fact must be in the answer, and at least 70% (COVER = 0.7) of the fact's stemmed content words must appear anywhere in it. Stop words, word order and inflection do not count. This is looser than word for word, so chance hits in a 1,000-character quote are more likely than that 'Known limits' line suggests.

Each fix is one line of text and needs no code change: 27 kinds; 8, or '7 to the fact route and 1 to the plan route'; '17 counting v2', or name the arms compared (v1, v13, quotes); and describe the scorer accurately. Parts (1) and (4) describe the questions and the measure in a preregistration that cannot be edited after the freeze. That is why I say fix before freezing, even though the severity is low.

(3) The seeds really were used. gen_counts.py calls fm.questions with seed 54, and multi50.py calls fm.questions(..., seed + 1), which gives 102-131. The only numbers missing from the list are 54 and 131, because 102-130 already fall inside '101-130'.

Why none of this harms the test:
(a) Nobody looked at test documents. The survey's outputs (gen_counts.json, proposals.json, multi50_sets.json) are aggregate counts and value distributions, so 'counts only' is accurate. These pool-wide counts are the same in every zone, because the zones are a random hash split, and the development zone was used for tuning anyway.
(b) schema.py sampled 300 documents per source from the whole corpus. It printed only the first non-empty example per field per source, at most 70 characters each: a handful of strings, and only some of them from documents now in the test zone. That is negligible.
(c) Deleting the cache protects nothing. The raw corpus (EnterpriseRAG-Bench/generated_data/sources, 3.7 GB) holds every test-zone document in full and has to stay for the test. zones.json.gz itself lists every test-zone id. brain_draw.planted_pairs and zone_pairs read test-zone GitHub and Linear documents by design. So 'no other scratch file holds a test-zone id' is false, and having code read test-zone documents is part of the protocol, not a breach of it. The real protection is the draw's PermissionError without the preregistered flag.
(d) Seeds 54 and 131 are survey seeds derived from the listed ones. They do not touch the test seeds 809-812.

Suggested fix (optional): edit the seed line to read 'a survey's counts over the whole fresh pool (before the split) and its draws 53/54 and 101-131, counts only', and note the change in the pre-freeze review section. This is not a must-fix before the freeze.

findings.title: The rule-router route count is wrong (8, not 7) and leaves out the single-document questions it sent to prose
findings.evidence: In v15a_rule.jsonl (and in v15base) the routes are ('prose','fact') 7 and ('prose','plan') 1, so 8 free-text questions took a fact route by the document's own definition in rule 7. The same router also sent 6 single-document questions to prose; the trained router sends none. The document says 'The rule router sent 7 free-text questions to a fact route.'
findings.fix: Say 8 of 52 (7 to the single-fact route, 1 to the planner), and add that the rule router sent 6 single-document questions to prose.

verdict.reason: I tried to refute this and could not; the finding holds. I counted routes by question family against /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/brain/dev5k/questions.jsonl. Both rule-router runs give the same free-text routes. v15base.jsonl has ('prose','fact') 7, ('prose','plan') 1 and ('prose','prose') 44. v15a_rule.jsonl has the same 7 / 1 / 44. The document's own definition is route_class() in cie/src/cie/eval/brain_test.py (lines 529-534). It maps every route other than not_found or prose to 'fact', so 'plan' counts as a fact route. That is also how rule 7 and ROUTE (line 51) score it. So the rule router sent 8 of 52 free-text questions to a fact route, not the 7 the document gives at FACTBANK_BRAIN_PREREGISTRATION.md lines 204-205. In both runs the rule router also sent 6 single-document questions to prose: ('single','prose') 6, with 106 single-document questions in total. The document never mentions this, at that line or in the 'Measured and dropped' line 220. The trained-router claims check out: v15a and v15b send 51 of 52 free-text questions to prose and 1 to fact, and send every single- and multi-document question to fact or plan, never to prose. The error is a descriptive count in the development section, which is seen and not results. It changes no rule, threshold, code path, seed or test outcome. Even the rule router's route accuracy, mean over families, would be about 0.95. So it does not have to be fixed before the freeze. It is a one-line correction to a document that becomes immutable, though, so fixing it is worthwhile: 8 of 52 (7 to the single-fact route, 1 to the planner), plus the 6 single-document questions sent to prose.

findings.title: The Disclosures leave out that the rules' margins and the test mix were set after the development scores were known, and one disclosure overstates what was developed on writer questions
findings.evidence: The rules and the mix were written after dev5k/report.json (21:20) and the frozen development scores. On development, single v15 0.804 vs v1 0.800 sits inside rule 1's -0.03, and free text 0.663 vs quotes 0.654 sits inside rule 3's -0.05. The mix copies the development mix with free text capped at 50; development had 52. The document says 'the descriptive checks were developed on writer questions from the same ten roles'. In fact brain_writers.py last changed in commit 92e5a03 at 20:31, the ten roles appear only in the train/dev writers workflow, and its outputs are dated 20:42. The checks were tuned on the training and development packets and on reviewer cases (build2_summary.txt), not on writer questions. The router was trained on writer questions.
findings.fix: Add to the Disclosures: 'The rules' margins and the test mix were chosen with the development scores known.' Reword the checks sentence: the descriptive checks were developed on the training and development packets before any writer question existed; the router was trained on the training writers' questions.

verdict.reason:
Only the narrow wording point holds. The rest of the finding is refuted.

CONFIRMED: the Disclosures sentence 'The router and the descriptive checks were developed on writer questions from the same ten roles' (FACTBANK_BRAIN_PREREGISTRATION.md, line 233-234) is wrong about the checks.
- cie/src/cie/eval/brain_writers.py, which holds collect and its checks, was changed only in commit 92e5a03 at 20:31:57. The working tree is clean.
- The only writer workflow on train/dev ran from 20:32:49 to 20:42:18. It is brain-writers-train-dev (wf_847b22c7-f99): 34 agents, with the ten roles. The batches are dated 20:32:37 and the outputs 20:42:26.
- No earlier writer workflow exists. The other runs that afternoon were brain-understand, brain-build-1 and brain-build-2.
- build2_summary.txt shows how the checks were developed: on the packets, on a code-generated 'simulated writer pass' (check_packets.py, whose simulated files were deleted) and on reviewer-made cases (reviewer_cases.py). No real writer question was involved.
- So no check was tuned on a writer question. The router was trained on them: its 111 free-text questions are the training writers' prose. The single and plan lessons were too: the 396 single questions include the 116 descriptive writer questions.
- The sentence therefore claims more dependence than there was. It is conservative and lets no one overclaim.

REFUTED: 'the margins and the mix were set after development scores and this is undisclosed'.
- The document opens by saying it was written after building and tuning v15 on training and development documents. The rules are part of that document.
- The −0.03 'not worse' and −0.05 margins are the repository's standing convention. They appear in FACTBANK_PREREGISTRATION, LEARNING, GENERAL, WORDS, LLM, PLAN, TICKET, ORDER, 5K, 5K_B and MEMORY_TEST. They were not tailored to the development scores.
- The development results pass with a margin of zero: 0.804 ≥ 0.800 on single and 0.663 ≥ 0.654 on free text. So the margins give the development set nothing.
- The test mix is stated as 'as in the development set'. That mix was fixed when dev5k/questions.jsonl was written at 20:43:49, before any development score (report.json at 21:20). The only change is free text at 50 instead of all 52. That cap does not bias a family mean.

Must not block the freeze. It is worth a one-line fix before freezing, since the text is then fixed for good. Suggested wording: the router and the single and plan lessons were trained on the training writers' questions; the descriptive checks were developed on the packets, simulated questions and reviewer cases before any writer question existed. No margin or mix disclosure is needed.
